summary.text: Coastal flooding happens when seawater covers dry, low-lying land.
Seawater can flood straight in, wash over a barrier or break through one, and how far inland it reaches depends on the shape of the land.
Rising seas, more extreme weather and growing coastal populations have made the damage from these floods worse and affected more people.

facts.value: Over 50 percent of the world's population

items.prompt: A seaside town pumps large amounts of water from wells near the shore for many years. How can this raise its flood risk?

options.label: The ground can sink lower over time
The nearby sea becomes much saltier
The local tides grow stronger
The offshore waves become taller

items.explain: Taking water out of coastal groundwater reservoirs can make the land subside, leaving it lower and easier to flood.

items.prompt: A town builds a sea wall to protect its main beach. What can this do to the stretch of coast next door?

options.label: Shield it from waves as well
Make it erode, raising its flood risk
Leave it completely unaffected
Build it up with extra sand

items.explain: Sea walls change the beach's natural processes, which can erode neighbouring coast and increase its flood risk.

items.prompt: During a storm, a strong wind blows from the sea toward the land for hours. What does this do to the water at the shore?

options.label: It lowers it by flattening the waves
It leaves the level unchanged
It piles the water up higher
It only raises water far offshore

items.explain: Onshore wind pushes water up against the coast, an effect called wind setup.

items.prompt: A deep low-pressure storm system sits over the ocean. What does the drop in air pressure do to the sea surface beneath it?

options.label: It sinks, because the air is lighter
It freezes into a thin crust
It stays flat, since air has no effect
It tends to rise higher

items.explain: Low atmospheric pressure in storms tends to raise the sea surface, which is called barometric setup.

items.prompt: Human-caused sea-level rise has changed how often historically rare extreme sea levels hit coasts. Since 1900, about how much more likely have they become?

options.label: About 10 percent more likely
About twice as likely
About four times as likely
About a hundred times as likely

items.explain: A 2026 study found these extreme coastal sea levels are roughly four times more likely than in 1900.

items.prompt: A coastal village wants to cut storm-wave damage without pouring concrete. Which step helps most?

options.label: Clearing shore plants so water drains
Keeping the mangrove forest on the shore
Draining wetlands to firm up the ground
Flattening dunes to widen the beach

items.explain: Mangroves and wetlands soak up wave energy and protect against storm waves, so natural defenses like these should be kept and protected.

pack.title: Three Ways the Sea Climbs
pack.question: What pushes seawater over coastal defenses during a storm?

beats.title: Three Ways the Sea Climbs
beats.hook: In a storm the sea rises by several separate tricks at once, and together they can send water over walls built to stop it.

beats.prompt: Match each storm condition to the rise in water it causes

left.label: Wind blowing from sea to land
Low air pressure in a storm
Taller breaking waves in the surf

beats.explain: Each condition lifts the water level at the coast in its own way, and the three interact to push seawater over barriers.

beats.prompt: A storm drives waves that are taller than the sea wall protecting a town. What happens?
beats.explain: When wave height exceeds the barrier, water flows over it and floods the land; these fast flows can even erode the ground and undermine the wall.

choices.label: Only spray gets over, so the land stays dry
choices.feedback: When wave height exceeds the barrier, real volumes of water flow over and flood.

choices.label: Water pours over the top and floods the land behind
The waves shrink as soon as they touch the wall
choices.feedback: Nothing about the wall makes the incoming waves smaller.

choices.label: The wall reflects every wave back out to sea
choices.feedback: A wall only stops water up to its own height; taller waves go over it.

left.label: Sea walls that erode nearby shores

right.label: Human change that can worsen flooding

beats.explain: Marshes, gravel bars and mangroves buffer the coast, while pumping groundwater can sink the land and sea walls can erode the coast next to them.

steps.text: Coastal flooding is largely a natural event.
Unusually high tides with strong winds and storm surges can flood coasts.
Because the causes are natural, changing the coast cannot make floods worse.
Rising seas and more people on coasts have made flood damage worse.

beats.explain: Human changes do make flooding worse: pumping coastal groundwater can sink the land, and sea walls can erode nearby coast.

beats.idea: Onshore wind, low air pressure and taller breaking waves each raise the water at the coast, and together they can carry seawater over barriers and inland.

paragraphs.heading: When the sea comes ashore
paragraphs.text: Coastal flooding is what happens when seawater spreads over land that is normally dry and sits low near the shore. How far the water gets inland depends on how high the floodwater rises and on the shape of the land it meets. The sea can get in by several routes: it can flow straight onto the land, spill over a barrier, or break through one. For the most part, this is a natural event.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters more now
paragraphs.text: The coastal zone is the strip of land within 100 kilometres of the coast and within 100 metres of sea level in height. More than half of the world's people live there, along with 65 percent of cities that have over five million people. Those coastal cities also produce a large share of the world's economic output, measured as Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Rising seas, more extreme weather and more people living by the coast have made flood damage worse and put more people in harm's way.

paragraphs.heading: What pushes the sea inland
paragraphs.text: Storm surges from hurricanes and tropical cyclones, sea-level rise driven by climate change, and tsunamis can all cause coastal floods. Unusually high tides, such as spring tides, can flood the coast too, especially when strong winds and storm surges add to them. That mix caused the North Sea flood of 1953, which put large parts of the Netherlands and the east coast of England under water. A 2026 study found that sea-level rise caused by people has made once-rare extreme coastal sea levels about four times more likely since 1900.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds of setup
paragraphs.text: Three effects can raise the water level at the shore. Wind blowing from the sea toward the land piles water up against the coast, which is called wind setup. The low air pressure that comes with storm systems lifts the sea surface, called barometric setup, and taller breaking waves raise the water in the surf zone, called wave setup. Working together, they can send waves over natural and built defences and carry seawater farther inland than usual.

paragraphs.heading: How people make it worse
paragraphs.text: Changes people make to the coast can make flooding worse. Pumping water out of underground stores near the coast can make the land sink, which raises the flood risk. Sea walls and other built defences change the natural workings of a beach. That can cause erosion on nearby stretches of coast, which also adds to the risk.

paragraphs.heading: Holding back the sea
paragraphs.text: Structural methods try to hold flood water back or send it somewhere else. Non-structural methods include coastal management and changes in how people and institutions respond. Nature offers defences too: gravel bars and sand dunes, and living systems such as salt marshes, seagrass and mangrove forests that act as a buffer. Mangroves, wetlands and seagrass meadows are often thought to give strong protection against storm waves, tsunamis and erosion by weakening wave energy. So keeping them healthy, for example inside Marine Protected Areas, helps guard the coast from floods.
